technique: sound — the consonants and vowels doing quiet work, worth saying aloud
lesson: Today we work on sound. Sound means the consonants and vowels in the words, and how they feel when you say them out loud. This poem leans on repeated consonant sounds. Listen for the s and sh sounds: "sharp at the window-crack where the sash won't seat." Say that line and your mouth makes a hissing noise, the same noise cold air makes through a gap. Listen for the k sounds too: "the kettle waits, the dog, the boots." Those hard sounds land like knocks. They make the line feel firm and physical, so you notice each object as a solid thing. The sound does part of the work the meaning does. Try this: pick one consonant and use it three or four times in a single line, then read it aloud to check it sounds right. The second time through, say the lines under your breath and feel which sounds are soft and which are hard. Here is the poem.
poem:
The cold has a smell before it has a shape—
woodsmoke that didn't all go up the flue,
and under it the apple-rot and leaf-mold
turning slow to dirt beneath the trees.
You wake into it, nose first, the room gone
sharp at the window-crack where the sash won't seat.
There's a whole list downstairs with your name worn into it,
small things that won't fix themselves, that wait
the way the kettle waits, the dog, the boots
stiff by the door and holding your shape in them.
And somewhere a phone will buzz with a question only
you can answer—not a chore, a hand held out.

Someone might want your little moose joke, a flower pressed flat, a few hands to clasp across a table—the day's got people in it, and they're worth walking toward.

So — up!
